newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-T&N sees brighter times in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-T&N sees brighter times in 1997.

text.p: British engineering group T&N Plc said on Thursday that 1997 looked positive after heavy losses in 1996, although currency movements and restructuring would continue to weigh on performance.
"The year has started on an encouraging note, with operating performance edging ahead," T&N chairman, Sir Colin Hope, told the annual meeting of shareholders.

Progress was still likely to be constrained to some degree by recent strength in sterling's exchange rate and a high level of restructuring, he said. But current sales volumes were in line with expectations, confirming some recovery in its markets, which centre on auto components.
T&N said with 25 percent of its manufacturing in the Britain, sterling's strength would continue to have some effect on performance, but that this was under control.

The company in March posted a 388 million pounds loss in 1996, after making exceptional charges of 515 million pounds to protect future results from its potential liabilities as the former Turner & Newall asbestos firm.
Chief executive Ian Much said the firm should bounce back following the setting up of the provision and additional insurance cover to meet any future asbestos claims.
"I feel good about the state of the business and the market," he told Reuters.
Hitherto the company had been taking an annual charge of around 50 million pounds to provide for asbestos claims, he said.
"We'll get the same type of profit as last year plus 50 million pounds because we won't be taking the asbestos charge," he said.
Meanwhile Hope denied T&N had any plans to sell its Ferodo brake products business despite recent press speculation.
The company announced earlier this year it was selling another business, its Flexitallic industrial seals unit for 42 million pounds, as part of its plan to raise funds to finance the asbestos fund.

It said in March it hoped to raise 70 million pounds for the fund this year from disposals of non-core businesses. "We will be examining the business to see if any more peripheral sections can go," Hope said.

But the company would continue to look for opportunities to expand its core operations and Hope said he remained confident over his long-running battle to take over German pistons maker Kolbenschmidt AG, adding that T&N's bid was far from over.

T&N has challenged a decision by Germany's cartel office to block its bid for Kolbenschmidt in favour of German industrial group Rheinmetall Berlin AG, and is now awaiting a ruling from a German appeals court.
"The act of being turned down is far from over, we're not unhappy with developments," he said.
Rheinmetall bought a 25 percent stake in Kolbenschmidt in March. The move was welcomed by Kolbenschmidt's management, but Hope has declined to say whether Rheinmetall was acting as a friend or foe.
"A good general doesn't tell the enemy what his next move is," he said.
However, Much said there were plenty of other opportunities if the Kolbenschmidt deal did not go through.
